sections.h2: What an Oklahoma sheriff sale is and who runs it
sections.html:
An Oklahoma sheriff sale is a public auction of real estate ordered by a court, and the county sheriff conducts it. Most home sales of this kind follow a mortgage foreclosure judgment, though a sheriff can also sell land to satisfy other money judgments.

Foreclosures here are mostly judicial. 12 O.S. section 686 allows real estate pledged as security to be sold only under a court judgment ordering the sale. When one mortgage covers land in two or more counties, the sheriff of each county sells the land in his or her own county.

The judgment also taxes costs, attorney fees and expenses and apportions them among the parties with liens. That is why the payoff by sale time is usually much larger than the missed payments alone.

sections.h2: How a sale is advertised and held
sections.html:
Notice goes out by mail and by publication before the sale. Under 12 O.S. section 764, the party who requested the sale must mail the sheriff's notice by first-class mail at least ten days before the sale to the judgment debtor and to every record lienholder whose interest the sale would wipe out, and must publish it for two successive weeks.

  • The mailed notice carries the legal description, date, time and place, and for an online sale, the internet address and bidding window.
  • If the county has no newspaper, notice also goes on the courthouse door and in five other public places.
  • In counties with 110,000 or more people, the ad runs in a newspaper in the city or township where the property lies.
  • An affidavit proving mailing and publication must be filed in the case.

If a bidder other than the foreclosing party fails to post the required ten percent within 24 hours, excluding Sundays and legal holidays, the sheriff may accept the next highest bid. A sale that skipped the statutory steps can be set aside on the court's motion.

sections.h2: How an Oklahoma County sale works
sections.html:
Oklahoma County runs its foreclosure sales online with Bid4Assets, on the second Tuesday of each month. The Oklahoma County Sheriff's page carries the rules a buyer must meet.

Buyer requirementOklahoma County rule
Sale formatVirtual auction, 10 a.m. Central, second Tuesday monthly
Minimum bidAt least two thirds of the appraised price
Down payment10 percent of the price within 24 hours
BalanceThe remaining 90 percent before the confirmation hearing
Payment formCertified funds payable to the Oklahoma County Court Clerk
Published listTwo consecutive weeks, at least 30 days before the sale

Bidders without internet access can request an offline paper bid packet from Bid4Assets. Properties sell as is, buyers must research liens, easements and encumbrances themselves, and bidders must be at least 18. Other counties may run things differently, since the statute leaves it to each sheriff whether to use an online marketplace.

sections.h2: What happens after the bidding ends?
sections.html:
The sale is not final until the court confirms it. Under 12 O.S. section 765, notice of the confirmation hearing must go by first-class mail at least ten days before the hearing to the same people who got the sale notice and to the high bidder.

Anyone who objects must file a written objection and mail a copy to those same parties before the hearing. The judge may continue the hearing so both sides can support or oppose the objection. If the court finds the sale followed the statute, it enters that finding on the journal and orders the officer to give the buyer a deed.

Meanwhile the purchase money sits with the court clerk until the judge has examined the proceedings, and then the clerk pays the person entitled to it. The statute also bars any buyer's premium on a sheriff sale. Once confirmed, the sheriff's deed conveys what the debtor could have conveyed and must be executed, acknowledged and recorded.

Counties generally record the deed within three weeks to three months of the sale, depending on local terms.

sections.h2: How long a homeowner can stay and what can stop the sale
sections.html:
A homeowner can generally stay until the court confirms the sale. Once the judgment is filed, the sheriff's sale is set for at least 30 days later, and confirmation comes at least ten days after the sale. Practice shifts over time, so confirm current timing with a lawyer.

Ways to avoid losing the home include:

  • Sell the house and pay off the loan, or ask the lender to approve a short sale if an offer falls short.
  • Pay a lump sum the lender's attorney will accept to reinstate, covering missed payments, taxes, insurance, court costs and attorney fees.
  • Offer a deed in lieu of foreclosure, which can bar collection of a deficiency.
  • Apply for a loan modification, which costs nothing to request.
  • File Chapter 13 bankruptcy, which can be filed until confirmation of the sale and requires regular income.

Legal Aid Services of Oklahoma may help eligible people with modification applications and Chapter 13 representation; its foreclosure guide walks through these options.

sections.h2: Can the lender collect more after the house sells for too little?
sections.html:
Only through a strict motion process. The lender must move for a post-judgment deficiency order with the motion to confirm or within 90 days of the sale, and the court then decides the fair market value of the property as of the sale date.

The deficiency order equals the debt with interest, plus costs and the amount owed on prior liens, less whichever is higher: the court's market value or the sale price. If no motion is filed, the sale proceeds count as full payment of the mortgage debt. For an owner facing a big gap between the loan and the house's value, that protection is a reason to attend the confirmation hearing or send a lawyer.

sections.h2: Sheriff sales versus tax resales and deed tax
sections.html:
A foreclosure sheriff sale and a county tax resale are different proceedings. Tax resales are run by the county treasurer on the second Monday of June for property with taxes unpaid three years or more, while a sheriff sale follows a court judgment on a mortgage or other debt.

Deed tax has its own rule. Under 68 O.S. section 3202, the documentary stamp tax does not apply to a foreclosure deed given to the mortgage holder who foreclosed. In other foreclosure actions the tax applies and the purchaser pays it, at $0.75 per $500 of consideration under section 3201.

sections.h2: Steps to take before a sale is scheduled
sections.html:
The window to act is widest before the judgment. After judgment a sale date follows quickly, and costs keep adding to the payoff.

An owner with equity may be able to sell traditionally. An owner with a house that needs repairs, carries liens or faces a tight deadline may look at a cash sale, where the buyer purchases as-is and closes through a title company that pays the lender from proceeds. Whether any route works depends on the loan balance, the court deadlines and the property's condition. This page is general information and not legal advice, so talk to an Oklahoma attorney or Legal Aid before deciding.

faqs.q: Is an Oklahoma sheriff sale final when the gavel falls?
faqs.a: No. The court must hold a confirmation hearing, with at least ten days' mailed notice, and approve the sale before the sheriff's deed issues.

faqs.q: How much do I need to bid at an Oklahoma sheriff sale?
faqs.a: The bid cannot be below two thirds of the appraised value. In Oklahoma County, ten percent is due within 24 hours and the remaining 90 percent before the confirmation hearing, paid in certified funds to the court clerk.

faqs.q: Can I stay in my house until the sheriff sale?
faqs.a: Generally yes. The homeowner may remain until confirmation of the sale, which occurs at least ten days after the sale.

faqs.q: Will I still owe money if the house sells for less than the loan?
faqs.a: Possibly. The lender must file a deficiency motion within 90 days of the sale, and if it does not, the sale proceeds count as full satisfaction of the mortgage debt.

faqs.q: Does the buyer at a sheriff sale pay a buyer's premium?
faqs.a: No. 12 O.S. section 765 bars any buyer's premium on a sale.
